title: The Longest Evenly Spaced Subsequence
statement:
A sequence is **arithmetic** if the difference between each two neighbouring numbers is the same (`4, 7, 10, 13` has the difference 3; a single number or two numbers are always arithmetic).

Find the **longest arithmetic subsequence** of `numbers`: you may delete any numbers but must keep the order of the rest. Return its length (`0` for an empty list).

hints.nudge: A subsequence is described by its last number and its difference. If you know the best length ending at an earlier number with the same difference, you can extend it. How would you store that?
hints.pattern: For each position j keep a hash map from a difference d to the length of the longest arithmetic subsequence that ENDS at j with difference d; compute it from every earlier position i.
hints.pseudocode:
best = min(n, 2)
for j in 0 .. n - 1:
  for i in 0 .. j - 1:
    d = numbers[j] - numbers[i]
    length[j][d] = length[i].get(d, 1) + 1
    best = max(best, length[j][d])
return best
hints.walkthrough: Trying all subsequences is exponential. Notice that two chosen numbers numbers[i] and numbers[j] fix the difference d = numbers[j] - numbers[i], and then the chain that ends at i with that same difference can be extended by j. So let length[j][d] be the longest arithmetic subsequence ending exactly at position j with difference d. For every earlier i: length[j][d] = length[i][d] + 1 if such a chain at i exists, and otherwise the pair (i, j) itself, which has length 2 (written as 1 + 1). A hash map per position stores only the differences that actually occur, so the memory is bounded by the number of pairs: O(n^2). The answer is the largest value anywhere (and n itself when n < 2).
